title: date and draft history
short: Written at Goslar in late 1798, sent to Coleridge in December 1798, and published in Lyrical Ballads (1800); probably the earliest of the 'Lucy poems'.
body: The Fenwick note says only 'Written in Germany, 1799', but the poem was in a letter to Coleridge in December 1798, where it is one of 'little Rhyme poems'. The draft had a final stanza in which the speaker tells Lucy of his fear, she laughs, and he now recalls the night with tears; Wordsworth cut it, ending on the unanswered fear. The text here is a later revision; the 1800 version read, for example, 'When she I lov'd, was strong and gay / And like a rose in June'.

title: fits of passion
short: Sudden attacks of strong feeling; 'fit' is a paroxysm, as of fever or madness.
body: A 'fit' (OED) is a sudden seizure, used of illness, emotion or madness; 'passion' is strong emotion, not only erotic love. The phrase presents the experience as involuntary and strange, a kind of mental episode. 'Fit' also had an old sense of a section of a ballad or song, and some readers hear a faint play on it at the opening of a ballad-like poem. The speaker addresses only 'the Lover's ear', claiming that only those in love will understand.

title: the lover as audience
short: The speaker will tell his story only to a fellow lover, as a secret confession.
body: The device creates intimacy and implies that the irrational fear he describes is common to lovers. It is also faintly self-ironic: 'dare to tell' makes a small confession sound like a perilous disclosure. 'Befel' (befell) means happened, a ballad word. The final stanza returns to the 'Lover's head', framing the poem. The convention of a tale told only to initiates also belongs to love-lyric tradition, in which lovers form a private community of understanding.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'befall, v.'
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

anchor: Fresh as a rose in June
title: 'Fresh as a rose in June'
short: A traditional ballad simile for a healthy young girl; in 1800 the line read 'And like a rose in June'.
body: The simile is a folk-song commonplace (compare Burns, 'O my Luve's like a red, red rose, / That's newly sprung in June', composed 1794). Wordsworth's 1800 text described Lucy as 'strong and gay', emphasizing her vitality, before the revision of 1836. The emphasis on her health 'every day' makes the speaker's sudden fear of her death irrational, the point of the poem.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem
Robert Burns, 'A Red, Red Rose' (1794)

title: the moon
short: The moon is the poem's central image: the rider fixes his eye on it as it sinks towards Lucy's cottage.
body: The moon is introduced as setting, then becomes the object of the rider's fixed gaze ('Upon the moon I fixed my eye'). Its gradual descent as the rider climbs the hill is an optical effect of perspective, but in the speaker's trance it acquires the force of an omen.

sources.cite: Geoffrey H. Hartman, Wordsworth's Poetry 1787-1814 (New Haven, 1964)
'The Lucy poems', Wikipedia (summary of the critical tradition: Hartman, Bateson, Ferry, Moorman, Jones)

title: lea
body: 'Lea' (OED) is a poetic word for meadow or pasture land, common in ballads and pastoral. With 'cot' (cottage), 'orchard-plot' and 'paths so dear' the vocabulary is deliberately simple and rustic, suited to Lyrical Ballads. The 'wide' lea contrasts with the narrowing focus on the cottage roof. The ride across open country towards a single point is the poem's whole structure: space contracts as the moon sinks, until both meet at the cottage.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'lea, n.1'

title: cot
short: Cottage; a poetic and rustic word. The name 'Lucy' first appears here.
body: 'Cot' is a short form of cottage, frequent in eighteenth-century pastoral verse (OED). In 1800 the lines read 'Towards the roof of Lucy's cot / The moon descended still'; the revision 'Came near, and nearer still' makes the moon seem to approach the house, intensifying the sense of fatal convergence. Naming Lucy at the moment the moon nears her home links the girl and the moon for the rest of the poem.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'cot, n.1'

title: 'In one of those sweet dreams I slept'
short: The rider falls into a waking dream while still watching the moon; the trance-like state explains the irrational fear.
body: The speaker is not literally asleep, for he keeps his eyes on the descending moon; he is in a reverie, a reverie. Sleep is 'Kind Nature's gentlest boon' (boon means gift or favour), an echo of the poetic tradition praising sleep. Critics have seen the passage as a study of how a mind absorbed in a monotonous rhythm and a single object can slip into associative fears. The motion of the horse ('hoof after hoof') prolongs the hypnotic state.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'boon, n.1'
Geoffrey H. Hartman, Wordsworth's Poetry 1787-1814 (New Haven, 1964)

title: 'hoof after hoof'
short: The rhythm imitates the steady, unbroken motion of the horse that lulls the rider.
body: The repetition 'hoof after hoof / He raised, and never stopped' enacts the monotony of the ride; the enjambment carries the motion across the line break. The steady motion is the precondition of the sudden shock in the next lines, where the moon drops 'At once'. The pattern of long continuity broken by a sudden event is typical of Wordsworth's 'spots of time', moments in which a small perception produces a disproportionate shock.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

title: 'At once, the bright moon dropped'
short: The moon suddenly vanishes behind the cottage roof, and the fear of Lucy's death strikes at the same instant.
body: As the rider nears the cottage, the roof hides the moon; a natural effect of perspective is felt as a blow. The pause after 'At once' and the plain verb 'dropped' make the moment abrupt. The moon's disappearance becomes an unspoken symbol of Lucy's life going out.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'planet, n.'

title: fond and wayward
short: 'Fond' here means foolish, as well as loving; 'wayward', wandering and wilful.
body: In older English 'fond' meant foolish or credulous (OED), and Wordsworth uses both senses: the thought is foolish because irrational, and loving because born of affection. 'Wayward' thoughts are those that turn aside from the expected path, as the mind does in reverie. The general reflection ('will slide / Into a Lover's head') returns to the audience of lovers addressed in the first stanza.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'fond, adj.'

title: 'If Lucy should be dead!'
short: The poem ends on the conditional fear, without telling us whether Lucy lived or died.
body: Wordsworth deleted the draft's final stanza, in which Lucy laughed at his fear and the speaker remembered the night with tears. Without it, the poem ends abruptly in the fear itself. Read alongside the other Lucy poems, where she does die, the cry seems a premonition; read alone, it is a psychological study of how love creates fear. Mark Jones's study of the Lucy poems shows how much the reading of each poem depends on the group into which editors have placed it.
